Given the following inspiring research papers:


### Paper 1:
**Wan: Open and Advanced Large-Scale Video Generative Models** (2025)
Research Question: How can large-scale, open, and efficient video generative models be developed to achieve superior performance, broad applicability, and resource efficiency across a wide range of video generation and editing tasks?
Hypothesis: Integrating a novel spatio-temporal variational autoencoder with scalable pre-training strategies, large-scale curated datasets, and advanced evaluation metrics will enable the development of video foundation models that surpass both open-source and commercial baselines in performance, versatility, and efficiency.
Proposed Method: A comprehensive suite of video generative models will be developed based on the diffusion transformer paradigm, incorporating a novel 3D causal spatio-temporal variational autoencoder (Wan-VAE) for efficient video compression and latent representation learning. The approach will utilize a multi-stage data curation pipeline to assemble billions of high-quality, diverse video and image samples, employing advanced filtering for visual and motion quality, text detection, and synthetic content removal. Dense video captioning will be enhanced through a LLaVA-style vision-language model, trained on both open-source and in-house datasets, to improve prompt alignment and downstream task performance. The models will be trained at multiple scales (1.3B and 14B parameters) using optimized parallelism, memory-efficient strategies, and post-training on curated high-fidelity data, supporting a range of applications including text-to-video, image-to-video, video editing, and real-time generation.
Novelty Claims: The proposal introduces the first open-source video foundation model suite capable of generating visual text in both Chinese and English, and supporting up to eight downstream applications. The spatio-temporal VAE architecture enables unprecedented compression and scalability for long video sequences. The data curation and captioning pipeline ensures high diversity and quality, while the models achieve state-of-the-art performance and efficiency, outperforming both open-source and commercial baselines. Full openness is claimed, with all code, models, and training pipelines to be released, fostering community advancement in large-scale video generation.


### Paper 2:
**Pyramidal Flow Matching for Efficient Video Generative Modeling** (2024)
Research Question: How can video generative modeling be made more computationally efficient while maintaining or improving the quality of generated videos, particularly for long-duration and high-resolution content?
Hypothesis: A unified pyramidal flow matching framework that leverages both spatial and temporal pyramid representations, jointly optimized in a single model, will significantly reduce computational and memory requirements for video generative modeling without compromising video quality.
Proposed Method: The proposed approach introduces a pyramidal flow matching algorithm that decomposes the video generation process into a series of pyramid stages, where only the final stage operates at full resolution. Each stage interpolates between compressed, noisy latents and cleaner, higher-resolution latents, using piecewise flow matching within defined time windows. The method jointly optimizes all pyramid stages using a unified flow matching objective in a single Diffusion Transformer (DiT), eliminating the need for separate models for each resolution. During inference, corrective Gaussian noise is added at stage transitions to maintain continuity of the probability path. Additionally, an autoregressive temporal pyramid is employed, conditioning the generation of future frames on a progressively compressed, lower-resolution history, further reducing token count and improving training efficiency.
Novelty Claims: The proposed method introduces a unified pyramidal flow matching framework that integrates both spatial and temporal pyramid representations within a single model, enabling end-to-end optimization and efficient knowledge sharing. Unlike cascaded approaches that require separate models for each resolution, this approach allows simultaneous generation and decompression across pyramid stages. The temporal pyramid further reduces redundancy in history conditioning, supporting efficient autoregressive video generation. The framework achieves state-of-the-art training efficiency and video quality among models trained on public data, and natively supports both text-to-video and text-conditioned image-to-video generation.


### Paper 3:
**Latte: Latent Diffusion Transformer for Video Generation** (2024)
Research Question: Can Transformer-based latent diffusion models be effectively leveraged to enhance the quality and realism of video generation, and what architectural and training practices yield optimal performance for such models?
Hypothesis: Transformer-based latent diffusion models, when equipped with efficient spatio-temporal decomposition, advanced patch embedding, adaptive information injection, and joint image-video training strategies, can outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in video generation tasks.
Proposed Method: A novel framework, Latte, will be developed that integrates a Transformer backbone within a latent diffusion model for video generation. Input videos will be encoded into a latent space using a pre-trained variational autoencoder, from which spatio-temporal tokens are extracted. Four model variants will be designed to efficiently decompose and capture spatial and temporal dependencies, including interleaved and late fusion Transformer blocks, as well as decomposed multi-head attention mechanisms. The method will systematically explore best practices for patch embedding (uniform vs. compression), timestep-class information injection (all tokens vs. scalable adaptive layer normalization), and temporal positional embedding (absolute vs. relative). Additionally, learning strategies such as initialization from pre-trained image models and joint image-video training with temporal masking will be incorporated to further enhance video quality and diversity.
Novelty Claims: The proposed research introduces the first comprehensive Transformer-based latent diffusion framework for video generation, featuring four efficient model variants for disentangling spatial and temporal information. It systematically investigates and establishes best practices for architectural design and training strategies specific to Transformer-based video diffusion models. The approach includes novel techniques for patch embedding, adaptive information injection, and joint image-video training with temporal masking. The method is expected to achieve state-of-the-art results on multiple video generation benchmarks and provide valuable insights for future research on integrating Transformers with diffusion models for video synthesis.


### Paper 4:
**Lumiere: A Space-Time Diffusion Model for Video Generation** (2024)
Research Question: How can video generation models synthesize realistic, diverse, and temporally coherent motion over entire video durations, and how can such models be extended to support a wide range of video content creation and editing tasks?
Hypothesis: A diffusion-based video generation model that processes the entire temporal duration of a video in a single pass, using a space-time U-Net architecture with both spatial and temporal down- and up-sampling, will produce videos with more globally coherent motion and higher visual quality than cascaded approaches that rely on generating keyframes and temporal super-resolution.
Proposed Method: A novel text-to-video diffusion model is proposed, built upon a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion backbone, and extended into a Space-Time U-Net (STUNet) architecture. This architecture interleaves temporal convolution and attention modules with spatial layers, enabling down- and up-sampling in both space and time, and allowing the model to process and generate the entire temporal span of a video in a single forward pass. The model generates low-resolution, full-frame-rate videos, which are then upsampled to high resolution using a spatial super-resolution (SSR) network applied on overlapping temporal windows. To ensure temporal consistency across these windows, a MultiDiffusion approach is employed, linearly combining predictions from overlapping segments. The method supports conditioning on text, images, masks, or style images, enabling applications such as text-to-video, image-to-video, inpainting, and stylized video generation.
Novelty Claims: The proposed approach introduces a space-time U-Net architecture that processes the full temporal duration of a video in a single pass, overcoming the limitations of cascaded keyframe and temporal super-resolution models in achieving global temporal coherence. The method leverages both spatial and temporal down- and up-sampling within the generative network, and extends MultiDiffusion to the temporal domain for seamless high-resolution video synthesis. The framework is designed to be flexible, supporting a wide range of video generation and editing applications, and demonstrates state-of-the-art results in both quantitative metrics and user preference studies.


### Paper 5:
**LTX-Video: Realtime Video Latent Diffusion** (2024)
Research Question: How can a unified, efficient, and high-quality video generation model be developed that supports both text-to-video and image-to-video tasks, while achieving real-time or faster-than-real-time performance and maintaining high visual fidelity and temporal consistency?
Hypothesis: Integrating the Video-VAE and denoising transformer into a holistic latent diffusion framework, with high spatiotemporal compression and novel loss functions, will enable faster-than-real-time video generation without sacrificing video quality or fine detail, outperforming existing models of similar scale.
Proposed Method: A transformer-based latent diffusion model will be developed that tightly integrates a high-compression Video-VAE and a denoising transformer. The Video-VAE will employ spatiotemporal downscaling (32×32×8 per token) and a high latent channel depth (128 channels), achieving a 1:192 compression ratio. The patchifying operation will be relocated from the transformer input to the VAE input, enabling the transformer to operate efficiently in a highly compressed latent space and perform full spatiotemporal self-attention. The VAE decoder will be tasked with both latent-to-pixel conversion and the final denoising step, producing clean results directly in pixel space and eliminating the need for a separate upsampling module. Additional architectural innovations include the use of rotary positional embeddings with normalized fractional coordinates, QK-normalization for attention stability, and a suite of novel loss functions (including a ReconstructionGAN and a spatiotemporal DWT loss) to enhance reconstruction quality and detail.
Novelty Claims: The proposed approach introduces a holistic integration of Video-VAE and transformer-based latent diffusion, optimizing their interaction for efficiency and quality. A novel high-compression Video-VAE architecture is developed, leveraging unique loss functions and multi-layer noise injection to enable unprecedented compression rates while maintaining video fidelity. The method eliminates the need for a separate upsampler by assigning the final denoising step to the VAE decoder, directly generating fine details in pixel space. Additional innovations include the use of ReconstructionGAN for improved adversarial training in reconstruction tasks and the application of advanced positional embeddings and attention normalization for robust spatiotemporal modeling. The resulting model achieves faster-than-real-time generation and sets a new benchmark for accessible, scalable video generation.

## Proposed Research

**Wan-Move: Motion-controllable Video Generation via Latent Trajectory Guidance** (2025)
Research Question: How can precise and scalable motion control be achieved in image-to-video generation models, enabling fine-grained and high-quality manipulation of object and camera motion in generated videos?
Hypothesis: Injecting motion guidance directly into the latent condition features of an image-to-video generation model, using dense point trajectories mapped into latent space, will enable precise, high-fidelity, and scalable motion control without requiring auxiliary motion encoders or architectural modifications.
Proposed Method: A novel framework is developed that represents object and camera motions using dense point trajectories, allowing for fine-grained control over scene dynamics. These trajectories are spatially mapped from pixel space into the latent space of a pretrained VAE, aligning with the latent representations used by the image-to-video (I2V) backbone. The first-frame latent features are then replicated along each trajectory across subsequent frames, producing a spatiotemporal feature map that encodes both appearance and motion. This updated latent condition is concatenated with the latent noise and injected into the I2V diffusion model (e.g., Wan-I2V-14B) as motion guidance, requiring no changes to the model architecture. The approach supports both single- and multi-object motion, as well as complex camera movements, and is compatible with scalable fine-tuning.
Novelty Claims: The proposed method introduces a simple yet effective approach for motion control in video generation by directly editing latent condition features, eliminating the need for auxiliary motion encoders or fusion modules. It enables scalable fine-tuning and seamless integration with existing I2V backbones. The framework supports diverse and complex motion control tasks, including multi-object and camera motion, with high fidelity and precision. A comprehensive benchmark, MoveBench, is also introduced, providing a rigorous evaluation platform with detailed motion annotations and diverse scenarios. The method achieves state-of-the-art results in both motion accuracy and video quality, rivaling commercial solutions while remaining open-source.
Experiment Details: Experiments are conducted using a large-scale, high-quality dataset of 2 million 720p videos, filtered for visual and motion consistency. The method is evaluated on the newly introduced MoveBench benchmark, which contains 1,018 videos (480x832 resolution, 5 seconds each) with rich, hybrid-verified motion annotations (point trajectories and masks) across 54 content categories, as well as on public datasets such as DAVIS. Baselines include state-of-the-art academic and commercial motion-controllable video generation methods (e.g., ImageConductor, LeviTor, Tora, MagicMotion, Kling1.5Pro). Evaluation metrics include FID, FVD, PSNR, SSIM for visual quality, and end-point error (EPE) for motion accuracy. Both quantitative and qualitative comparisons are performed, including ablation studies on motion guidance strategies, condition fusion, and the number of point trajectories. Human studies (2AFC) are conducted to assess motion and visual quality.

Target Research Question: How can fine-grained 3D geometry and semantic occupancy of complex driving scenes be accurately and efficiently predicted from multi-camera images, particularly addressing the challenges posed by both static and dynamic scene elements?

Given the following inspiring research papers:


### Paper 1:
**3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering** (2023)
Research Question: How can real-time, high-quality novel view synthesis of complex 3D scenes from multi-view images be achieved, overcoming the trade-off between rendering speed and visual fidelity that limits current radiance field methods?
Hypothesis: A scene representation based on anisotropic 3D Gaussians, optimized with adaptive density control and rendered via a fast, differentiable, visibility-aware rasterizer, will enable real-time, high-quality radiance field rendering with training and inference speeds competitive with or superior to existing methods.
Proposed Method: The proposed approach represents a scene as a set of anisotropic 3D Gaussians, initialized from sparse points obtained via Structure-from-Motion (SfM) from multi-view images. Each Gaussian is parameterized by its 3D position, anisotropic covariance (decomposed into scale and rotation), opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients for view-dependent color. Optimization proceeds by interleaving stochastic gradient descent updates of these parameters with adaptive density control: Gaussians are cloned or split based on view-space positional gradients to populate under- or over-reconstructed regions, and transparent or oversized Gaussians are periodically culled. Rendering is performed using a custom, tile-based, differentiable rasterizer that projects and sorts Gaussians for efficient alpha-blending, supporting anisotropic splats and unlimited depth complexity for gradient computation. The rasterizer is fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end optimization of the scene representation.
Novelty Claims: The proposed method introduces a novel, unstructured scene representation using anisotropic 3D Gaussians for radiance fields, enabling both high-quality and real-time rendering. Key innovations include an adaptive density control mechanism interleaved with parameter optimization, a fast tile-based differentiable rasterizer supporting visibility-aware anisotropic splatting, and the ability to handle unlimited depth complexity during gradient computation. The approach achieves state-of-the-art visual quality with training and inference speeds that match or exceed the fastest prior methods, and is the first to enable real-time, high-fidelity novel view synthesis for complex, unbounded scenes at 1080p resolution.


### Paper 2:
**A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets** (2024)
Research Question: How can real-time rendering of extremely large 3D scenes, captured from thousands of images over kilometer-scale trajectories, be achieved with high visual quality and efficient resource usage?
Hypothesis: A hierarchical 3D Gaussian representation, combined with a divide-and-conquer training approach and optimized level-of-detail (LOD) selection, will enable real-time rendering of very large datasets while preserving visual quality and allowing scalable resource usage.
Proposed Method: The proposed method introduces a hierarchical framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), enabling efficient level-of-detail rendering of massive scenes. The scene is first subdivided into manageable chunks, each trained independently using an adapted 3DGS optimization that accounts for sparse and large-scale data. For each chunk, a tree-based hierarchy is constructed, merging 3D Gaussian primitives into interior nodes using geometric and appearance-based criteria, and supporting efficient cut selection and smooth transitions between LODs. The method further optimizes the attributes of intermediate nodes in the hierarchy, using a full-resolution, multi-granularity training regime that preserves high-frequency details and enables robust anti-aliasing. After per-chunk optimization, hierarchies are consolidated into a global structure, with redundant nodes pruned and cross-chunk consistency enforced, enabling real-time LOD-based rendering of the entire scene.
Novelty Claims: The method introduces the first hierarchical 3D Gaussian representation supporting dynamic level-of-detail rendering for extremely large scenes. It enables divide-and-conquer training and parallel processing of scene chunks, scalable to tens of thousands of images and multi-kilometer trajectories. The approach includes a novel hierarchy construction and optimization scheme that preserves high-frequency details at all levels, robust anti-aliasing, and smooth LOD transitions. The solution is the first to demonstrate real-time rendering of radiance fields at this scale, with resource-adaptive behavior and compatibility with affordable consumer capture rigs. Planned public release of code and large-scale datasets further contributes to the field.


### Paper 3:
**MVSplat: Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting from Sparse Multi-View Images** (2024)
Research Question: How can high-quality 3D scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis be achieved efficiently from sparse multi-view images, using a lightweight and fast feed-forward model?
Hypothesis: A feed-forward model that leverages multi-view cost volume representations for feature matching can more accurately localize 3D Gaussian primitives, resulting in improved geometry and appearance quality, faster inference, and better generalization compared to existing methods that regress depth directly from image features.
Proposed Method: The proposed approach introduces a feed-forward framework for 3D scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis from sparse multi-view images by predicting 3D Gaussian parameters. Multi-view image features are first extracted using a combination of a shallow CNN and a multi-view Transformer with self- and cross-attention layers. For each input view, a cost volume is constructed via plane sweeping, capturing cross-view feature similarities across sampled depth candidates. These cost volumes are refined using a 2D U-Net with cross-view attention, and per-view depth maps are estimated via softmax-weighted averaging over depth candidates. The predicted depths are unprojected to form 3D Gaussian centers, while opacity, covariance, and color parameters are predicted jointly using convolutional layers. The entire model is trained end-to-end using only photometric supervision, with rendered images compared to ground truth using a combination of L2 and LPIPS losses.
Novelty Claims: The method introduces a cost volume-based feature matching approach for efficient and accurate localization of 3D Gaussian centers, enabling high-quality geometry and appearance from sparse views. It achieves state-of-the-art performance with 10× fewer parameters and more than 2× faster inference compared to the strongest baseline, while requiring only photometric supervision and no ground truth geometry. The approach generalizes across datasets and demonstrates superior efficiency and reconstruction quality, particularly in challenging and ambiguous regions.


### Paper 4:
**OccFormer: Dual-path Transformer for Vision-based 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction** (2023)
Research Question: How can vision-based systems for autonomous driving achieve more accurate and efficient 3D semantic occupancy prediction from camera images, overcoming the limitations of existing BEV and 3D convolutional approaches?
Hypothesis: A dual-path transformer network that decomposes 3D feature processing into local and global pathways, combined with transformer-based mask classification and specialized pooling and sampling strategies, will enable more accurate and efficient 3D semantic occupancy prediction from camera images than existing methods.
Proposed Method: A novel dual-path transformer framework, OccFormer, will be developed for vision-based 3D semantic occupancy prediction. The method begins with an image encoder (e.g., EfficientNetB7 or ResNet-101) to extract multi-scale 2D features from monocular or multi-camera images. These features are lifted to a 3D voxel feature volume using a depth distribution and voxel pooling mechanism inspired by LSS. The dual-path transformer encoder processes the 3D volume: the local path applies shared windowed self-attention to each horizontal slice for fine-grained semantic extraction, while the global path aggregates scene-level semantics via average pooling along the height and ASPP modules. Outputs from both paths are fused using a sigmoid-weighted summation. For decoding, a transformer-based occupancy decoder adapts Mask2Former for 3D, introducing preserve-pooling (max-pooling for mask downsampling) and class-guided sampling (sampling voxels based on class frequency) to address sparsity and class imbalance. The final occupancy prediction is formulated as a set of mask classification queries over the 3D voxel grid.
Novelty Claims: The proposed approach introduces the first dual-path transformer encoder for efficient and dynamic 3D feature processing in vision-based semantic occupancy prediction. It is also the first to adapt transformer-based mask classification (Mask2Former) to 3D occupancy, with novel modifications including preserve-pooling for sparse mask downsampling and class-guided sampling to address class imbalance. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on SemanticKITTI for semantic scene completion and on nuScenes for camera-based LiDAR segmentation, outperforming both monocular and multi-view baselines. The dual-path design and tailored decoder strategies provide significant improvements in efficiency, accuracy, and the ability to recover fine-grained and scene-level semantics from camera images.


### Paper 5:
**SurroundOcc: Multi-Camera 3D Occupancy Prediction for Autonomous Driving** (2023)
Research Question: How can dense and accurate 3D occupancy of real-world scenes be predicted using only multi-camera images, in a way that generalizes to arbitrary object shapes and classes for autonomous driving applications?
Hypothesis: A multi-camera vision-based approach utilizing 2D-3D spatial attention and a novel dense occupancy ground truth generation pipeline can achieve superior 3D occupancy prediction performance compared to existing methods relying on sparse LiDAR supervision or BEV-based representations.
Proposed Method: A new framework is developed for multi-camera 3D occupancy prediction. The approach begins by extracting multi-scale features from each camera image using a 2D backbone network (e.g., ResNet-101 or EfficientNetB7 with FPN). These features are lifted to 3D volumetric space using a 2D-3D spatial attention mechanism based on deformable attention, which projects 3D reference points into 2D views and aggregates information from relevant image regions. The resulting 3D volume features are progressively upsampled and fused via a 3D convolutional U-Net-like architecture, with multi-scale skip connections to preserve both high- and low-level details. Supervision is imposed at multiple levels using a decayed weighted loss. To enable dense occupancy prediction, a pipeline is designed to generate dense ground truth by fusing multi-frame LiDAR scans of dynamic objects and static scenes, applying Poisson surface reconstruction to fill holes, voxelizing the resulting mesh, and assigning semantic labels via nearest neighbor search.
Novelty Claims: The proposed method introduces a novel 2D-3D spatial attention mechanism for fusing multi-camera image features directly into 3D volumetric space, preserving geometric consistency and enabling prediction of occluded regions. A new pipeline for generating dense 3D occupancy ground truth from sparse LiDAR and existing annotations is developed, leveraging multi-frame fusion, Poisson reconstruction, and semantic label propagation. The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on both multi-camera and monocular 3D semantic scene completion and reconstruction benchmarks, and demonstrates significant improvements in occupancy density and accuracy over prior methods. The framework is also efficient and extensible to downstream 3D tasks.

## Proposed Research

**ODG: Occupancy Prediction Using Dual Gaussians** (2025)
Research Question: How can fine-grained 3D geometry and semantic occupancy of complex driving scenes be accurately and efficiently predicted from multi-camera images, particularly addressing the challenges posed by both static and dynamic scene elements?
Hypothesis: Decomposing driving scenes into static and dynamic components and modeling them with dedicated dual sets of Gaussian queries, combined with hierarchical coarse-to-fine prediction and multi-stage rendering supervision, will improve 3D occupancy prediction accuracy and efficiency over existing methods.
Proposed Method: A dual-query architecture will be designed, introducing two distinct sets of 3D Gaussian queries to separately model static background elements and dynamic agents within driving scenes. Each Gaussian is parameterized by mean, scale, rotation, and opacity, with dynamic Gaussians further augmented with 3D bounding box attributes and velocity vectors to capture object motion. A hierarchical, coarse-to-fine transformer-based refinement will be employed, allowing a large number of Gaussians to be predicted across multiple layers, thus increasing model capacity and expressiveness. Attention mechanisms, specifically self-attention over concatenated dynamic and static query features, will facilitate rich information exchange between the two query types. Multi-stage real-time rendering supervision using 3D Gaussian Splatting will be imposed, leveraging available depth and semantic map annotations from projected LiDAR points to enforce pixel-level alignment and improve spatial coherence.
Novelty Claims: The proposal introduces a novel dual Gaussian query design that explicitly separates static and dynamic scene modeling, enhancing the handling of dynamic agents. Hierarchical coarse-to-fine prediction enables the use of a much larger number of Gaussians, increasing model expressiveness. A new self-attention mechanism across concatenated dynamic and static queries is proposed to facilitate effective information sharing. Multi-stage rendering supervision with 3D Gaussian Splatting injects pixel-level alignment and spatial consistency, improving learning from both 2D and 3D labels. The overall framework is claimed to achieve new state-of-the-art results in 3D occupancy prediction while maintaining competitive inference efficiency.
Experiment Details: Experiments will be conducted on the Occ3D-nuScenes and Occ3D-Waymo benchmarks, which provide annotated 3D occupancy ground-truth and semantic labels for urban driving scenes. The evaluation will use metrics such as mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and RayIoU, with model performance compared against state-of-the-art baselines including OPUS, GaussRender, SparseOcc, and others. Implementation will utilize a ResNet-50 backbone for image feature extraction, hierarchical transformer layers for Gaussian prediction, and rendering supervision at multiple stages. Both small and large model variants will be tested, using standard training protocols, batch sizes, and inference-time visibility masks. Ablation studies will analyze the impact of motion compensation, query interaction mechanisms, and rendering supervision on model performance.

Target Research Question: How can the evaluation of individual neuron explanations in neural networks be standardized and improved to ensure reliability and faithfulness across different domains and explanation types?

Given the following inspiring research papers:


### Paper 1:
**Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons** (2023)
Research Question: How can the faithfulness of natural language explanations for individual neurons in large language models be rigorously evaluated, and to what extent do such explanations accurately reflect both the encoding and causal mediation of linguistic concepts within neural activations?
Hypothesis: Natural language explanations of individual neurons in large language models are not reliably faithful to the actual neural activations and do not generally correspond to causal mediators of the concepts they purport to explain.
Proposed Method: A two-pronged evaluation framework will be developed for assessing natural language explanations of neurons. The first component, observational evaluation, will test whether a neuron's activation aligns with the set of input strings denoted by a proposed explanation, quantifying precision, recall, and F1-score over curated datasets. The second component, intervention-based evaluation, will use causal mediation analysis via interchange interventions: neuron activations will be manipulated during model inference to determine if such interventions causally affect model outputs in tasks dependent on the explained concept. Both single neuron and multi-neuron (probe-based) settings will be considered, and the evaluation will be applied to explanations generated by large language models (e.g., GPT-4) for neurons in a pretrained language model such as GPT-2 XL.
Novelty Claims: The proposed framework introduces a rigorous, dual-mode evaluation for natural language explanations of neurons, combining direct observational testing with causal intervention analysis. This approach goes beyond previous neuron-level metrics by explicitly quantifying both faithfulness to neuron activations and causal efficacy in model behavior. The methodology also highlights inherent limitations of natural language as an explanatory medium and questions the appropriateness of individual neurons as the primary unit of interpretability, offering critical insights for the development of more robust and actionable model explanations.


### Paper 2:
**CoSy: Evaluating Textual Explanations of Neurons** (2024)
Research Question: How can the quality of textual explanations for neurons in deep neural networks be quantitatively and automatically evaluated in a unified, architecture-agnostic manner, particularly for open-vocabulary explanations in computer vision models?
Hypothesis: A generative-model-based evaluation framework that synthesizes visual representations from textual neuron explanations and quantitatively compares neuron activations on these versus control images can provide a reliable, general-purpose measure of explanation quality, enabling robust benchmarking across explanation methods and model architectures.
Proposed Method: The proposed methodology introduces an automatic evaluation framework (COSY) for textual explanations of neurons. The approach consists of three main steps: (1) For each neuron and its associated textual explanation, a generative text-to-image model is used to synthesize a set of images representing the explanation. (2) The neuron’s activations are collected for both the synthetic images and a control dataset of natural images unrelated to the explanation. (3) The quality of the explanation is quantified by comparing the distributions of neuron activations on the synthetic and control images using metrics such as Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) and Mean Activation Difference (MAD). The method is architecture-agnostic and can be applied to any computer vision model and explanation method, leveraging recent advances in generative AI to bridge the gap between textual and visual domains.
Novelty Claims: The proposed framework is the first general-purpose, quantitative, and architecture-agnostic method for evaluating textual explanations of neurons, enabling direct benchmarking across different explanation methods and models. It leverages generative models to synthesize visual representations from open-vocabulary textual explanations, facilitating a unified evaluation approach that does not require human annotation or ground truth labels for latent neurons. The framework provides new insights into the reliability and limitations of existing neuron explanation methods, particularly highlighting the challenges in explaining lower-layer neurons and the variability in explanation quality across methods.


### Paper 3:
**FIND: A Function Description Benchmark for Evaluating Interpretability Methods** (2023)
Research Question: How can the evaluation of automated interpretability methods for neural network submodules be systematically benchmarked using functions with known structure across diverse domains, and what are the limitations of current large language model-based approaches in generating accurate, human-legible descriptions of such functions?
Hypothesis: Automated interpretability agents, particularly those leveraging large language models, can generate accurate and human-interpretable descriptions of black-box functions across numeric, string, and semantic domains when provided with a comprehensive benchmark; however, these agents may exhibit systematic limitations in capturing local details and complex behaviors without additional tools or targeted evaluation protocols.
Proposed Method: A comprehensive benchmark suite, FIND (Function INterpretation and Description), will be constructed by procedurally generating over 2000 function interpretation problems spanning numeric operations, string manipulations, and synthetic neural modules that mimic real-world neural network behaviors. Each function will be implemented as an independent Python script, allowing black-box access for interpreters, and will include both atomic and composed functions, with complexity introduced via composition, noise, domain corruption, and approximation. Automated interpretability agents, powered by large language models, will interact with these functions by selecting inputs, observing outputs, and iteratively updating hypotheses to produce structured descriptions in both code and natural language. Evaluation protocols will include both code-based and language-based assessments, with interpreters required to approximate function behavior, identify domain-specific anomalies, and articulate underlying rules or concepts.
Novelty Claims: The proposed benchmark provides the first large-scale, extensible suite for evaluating automated interpretability methods on functions with known ground-truth structure, enabling systematic and reproducible assessment of both code- and language-based explanations. The approach introduces interactive interpretability agents that autonomously generate and test hypotheses about black-box functions, moving beyond static exemplar-based evaluation. FIND supports targeted evaluation of interpreters' abilities to identify domain-specific anomalies, compositional structure, and noise models, and is designed to evolve with the field by incorporating new function types, interaction paradigms, and evaluation metrics. This work aims to drive the development of more robust, general-purpose interpretability tools and to reveal the current limitations of LM-based agents in automated model interpretation.


### Paper 4:
**Labeling Neural Representations with Inverse Recognition** (2023)
Research Question: How can neural representations within deep neural networks be systematically labeled and interpreted in terms of human-understandable concepts, without reliance on segmentation masks or high computational cost, and with statistical significance guarantees?
Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that neural representations can be effectively and efficiently explained by identifying compositional concepts that maximize their discriminative capacity, as measured by a robust similarity metric, and that these explanations can be made statistically significant and interpretable without requiring segmentation masks.
Proposed Method: A scalable framework is developed for labeling neural representations by leveraging their ability to discriminate between human-understandable concepts, using only labeled data. The method defines neural representations as scalar functions over the data domain and concepts as binary functions corresponding to labeled attributes. The core approach involves searching for compositional concepts—logical combinations of atomic concepts (using AND, OR, NOT)—that maximize the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUC) similarity between the representation and the concept. Beam search is employed to efficiently explore the space of compositional concepts up to a predetermined formula length, with constraints on the fraction of data points covered by the concept to balance precision and generality. Statistical significance of the resulting explanation is assessed using the Mann–Whitney U test, reporting p-values to ensure the robustness of the explanation.
Novelty Claims: The proposed approach eliminates the need for segmentation masks and is applicable to diverse neuron types, reducing computational complexity compared to prior methods. It introduces an interpretable similarity metric (AUC) for explanation quality, incorporates statistical significance testing for explanation robustness, and supports compositional explanations using logical operators. The method enables efficient model auditing for spurious correlations, facilitates circuit-level interpretability, and allows for the manual construction of symbolic-like circuits from neural representations. Empirical results demonstrate superior or comparable explanation accuracy and significantly reduced computational cost relative to established baselines.


### Paper 5:
**Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing** (2023)
Research Question: How are high-level, human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of large language models, and how does the sparsity and localization of these representations vary with model scale and feature type?
Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that certain features are represented sparsely and can be localized to individual or small subsets of neurons, with representational sparsity increasing as model scale grows. Additionally, it is expected that early layers utilize superposition to encode many features, while middle layers may contain more monosemantic neurons dedicated to higher-level contextual features.
Proposed Method: A methodology will be developed to train k-sparse linear probes on the internal activations of transformer-based large language models (LLMs), focusing primarily on the activations of multi-layer perceptron (MLP) layers. The probes will be constrained to use at most k neurons to predict the presence of specific, human-interpretable features in the input. Two main sparse feature selection techniques will be implemented: optimal sparse probing (OSP), which uses a cutting-plane algorithm to provably select the best k neurons for small k, and adaptive thresholding, which iteratively reduces k by selecting top neurons based on coefficient magnitude. Probing datasets will be carefully constructed to ensure conceptual separation between features and their correlates, and aggregation strategies (e.g., mean or max over token spans) will be used for sequence-level features. Logistic regression will be used as the base classifier for all probes.
Novelty Claims: The proposed approach introduces a systematic framework for localizing features to individual or sparse subsets of neurons in LLMs using provably optimal sparse probing techniques. The methodology enables precise identification of both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons, and provides empirical evidence of superposition and its scaling dynamics in real-world LLMs. The work addresses key limitations of previous probing studies by leveraging sparsity as an inductive bias, improving interpretability, and offering new tools for refining and verifying neuron-feature associations. This framework is expected to advance mechanistic interpretability by revealing the structure and scaling behavior of feature representations in large language models.

Research Question: How can the evaluation of individual neuron explanations in neural networks be standardized and improved to ensure reliability and faithfulness across different domains and explanation types?
Hypothesis: A unified mathematical framework for evaluating neuron explanations, combined with rigorous sanity checks, will enable the identification of reliable evaluation metrics and expose weaknesses in commonly used metrics.
Proposed Method: A unified evaluation framework, termed NeuronEval, will be developed to formalize and encompass a wide range of existing neuron explanation evaluation metrics under a single mathematical notation. This framework will represent evaluation as a function of neuron activation vectors and concept activation vectors, allowing for the systematic comparison and analysis of 18+ metrics, including Recall, Precision, F1-score, IoU, Correlation, AUPRC, and others. Two novel sanity checks, the Missing Labels Test and Extra Labels Test, will be introduced to assess whether evaluation metrics can distinguish between explanations that are too specific or too generic, respectively. Both theoretical and empirical analyses will be conducted, including the derivation of analytical expectations and the implementation of these tests on real and synthetic neuron/concept pairs. The approach will also include meta-evaluation by measuring how well each metric separates correct from incorrect explanations using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) across multiple datasets and domains.
Novelty Claims: The proposed research introduces the first unified mathematical framework (NeuronEval) that encompasses nearly all existing neuron explanation evaluation metrics, enabling direct comparison and systematic analysis. Two new sanity checks (Missing Labels Test and Extra Labels Test) are proposed to rigorously assess the reliability of evaluation metrics, revealing that many widely used metrics fail at least one of these basic tests. The research identifies a set of reliable metrics (Correlation, Cosine Similarity, F1-score, IoU, AUPRC) and provides clear guidelines for future evaluation practices. The approach also connects common explanation failure modes to the proposed tests, offering a principled foundation for trustworthy neuron explanation evaluation.
Experiment Details: Experiments will be conducted on a diverse set of neural network models, including vision models (evaluated on ImageNet, Places365, and CUB200 datasets) and language models (evaluated on OpenWebText). Both final layer and hidden layer neurons, as well as CBM neurons and linear probe outputs, will be included. Evaluation metrics will be tested using both ground truth and pseudo-labels as concept sources. For each metric, the Missing Labels and Extra Labels sanity checks will be applied, and DecreaseAcc (the proportion of neurons where the metric decreases as expected) will be reported. Additionally, meta-evaluation will be performed by computing the AUPRC for each metric's ability to rank correct explanations above incorrect ones for neurons with known ground truth concepts. Hyperparameters for metrics will be selected using a validation split, and results will be averaged across multiple experimental setups. Ablation studies and sensitivity analyses will be included to ensure robustness.

Target Research Question: How can small language models be more effectively aligned with human preferences using preference distillation, especially when limited to coarse-grained, binary feedback and lacking the capacity to fully leverage large teacher models?

Given the following inspiring research papers:


### Paper 1:
**Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model** (2023)
Research Question: How can language models be fine-tuned to align with human preferences in a manner that is stable, efficient, and avoids the complexity and instability of reinforcement learning-based approaches?
Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that a direct optimization approach, which parameterizes the reward model such that the optimal policy can be extracted in closed form and optimized with a simple classification loss, can match or outperform reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) methods in aligning language models with human preferences, while being more stable and computationally efficient.
Proposed Method: A new algorithm, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), will be developed to fine-tune language models directly from human preference data without explicit reward modeling or reinforcement learning. The method leverages a reparameterization of the reward function, enabling the extraction of the optimal policy in closed form under a Bradley-Terry or Plackett-Luce preference model. The DPO objective is formulated as a binary cross-entropy loss over preference pairs, where the policy network represents both the language model and an implicit reward model. The update rule increases the log-probability of preferred responses relative to dispreferred ones, with a dynamic per-example importance weighting that prevents model degeneration. The reference policy is initialized from a supervised fine-tuned (SFT) model or by maximizing the likelihood of preferred completions, and the DPO loss is minimized over the preference dataset using standard gradient-based optimization.
Novelty Claims: The proposed method eliminates the need for explicit reward modeling and reinforcement learning in preference-based fine-tuning of language models, instead optimizing a theoretically equivalent objective via a simple classification loss. The approach provides a closed-form mapping from reward functions to optimal policies, enabling efficient and stable optimization. DPO is claimed to match or exceed the performance of PPO-based RLHF in tasks such as sentiment control, summarization, and dialogue, while being computationally lightweight, robust to hyperparameter choices, and easier to implement and train. The method offers new theoretical insights into the equivalence of reward and policy parameterizations in preference learning, and demonstrates strong empirical performance and generalization.


### Paper 2:
**From $r$ to $Q^*$: Your Language Model is Secretly a Q-Function** (2024)
Research Question: Can direct preference optimization (DPO) be theoretically and practically formulated as a token-level Q-learning algorithm for large language models, and does this formulation enable improved alignment, credit assignment, and decoding strategies in generative AI systems?
Hypothesis: Direct preference optimization can be cast as a general inverse Q-learning algorithm at the token-level, enabling language models to implicitly learn optimal Q-functions for arbitrary dense reward functions, thereby supporting improved credit assignment and more effective decoding strategies such as beam search.
Proposed Method: A novel theoretical framework will be developed to derive direct preference optimization (DPO) within the token-level Markov Decision Process (MDP) for large language models. This approach will establish a bijection between reward functions and optimal Q-functions, showing that the language model's logits correspond to the optimal Q-function under a suitable reward. The method will further demonstrate that DPO can parameterize any dense reward function via optimal advantage functions, and that the DPO loss can be reformulated in terms of token-level preferences. Empirical analysis will be conducted to validate the ability of DPO to perform per-token credit assignment, and to connect likelihood-based decoding (e.g., beam search) with reward-guided search in the token-level MDP. The impact of reference policy selection on implicit reward dynamics during training will also be explored.
Novelty Claims: The proposed research provides the first theoretical derivation of DPO as a token-level Q-learning algorithm, establishing a direct connection between language model logits and optimal Q-functions for arbitrary dense reward functions. It demonstrates that DPO can perform per-token credit assignment from trajectory-level feedback, unifies likelihood-based decoding with reward-guided search, and explains empirical phenomena such as decreasing likelihoods during DPO training. The work offers a unified framework for understanding and improving direct alignment methods in generative AI, with implications for multi-turn dialogue, agentic LLMs, and end-to-end training of multi-modal generative systems.


### Paper 3:
**Robust Preference Optimization through Reward Model Distillation** (2024)
Research Question: How can the robustness and effectiveness of language model alignment with human preferences be improved, particularly in offline settings where preference data may be biased or limited?
Hypothesis: Explicitly distilling reward models into the policy, and further incorporating pessimism over a family of plausible reward models, will yield more robust and effective preference optimization than direct preference optimization alone, especially under distribution shift or bias in preference annotations.
Proposed Method: A novel framework is proposed that distills the knowledge of an explicit reward model, trained on preference data, into the language model policy. The approach optimizes a squared loss that matches the pairwise differences in reward scores between generation pairs, aligning the policy's implicit reward with the explicit reward model. To address uncertainty in the reward model, a pessimistic extension is introduced: the policy is trained to maximize the worst-case improvement across a set of plausible reward models, effectively regularizing against overfitting to any single reward function. This pessimistic distillation is implemented by augmenting the distillation loss with a forward KL-divergence penalty between the policy and a reference model, and can be extended to ensembles of reward models to further enhance robustness.
Novelty Claims: The proposed method introduces reward model distillation for offline preference optimization, bridging the gap between supervised direct preference optimization and explicit reward modeling. The pessimistic extension, which optimizes for the worst-case reward over a set of plausible models, provides a principled mechanism for handling uncertainty and distribution shift in preference data. The approach maintains the simplicity and efficiency of offline alignment while offering improved robustness and theoretical guarantees against degeneracy and overfitting observed in prior methods. Empirical results demonstrate significant improvements over existing offline alignment techniques, especially in the presence of biased or challenging preference distributions.


### Paper 4:
**SimPO: Simple Preference Optimization with a Reference-Free Reward** (2024)
Research Question: How can preference optimization for large language models be improved to achieve better alignment with human feedback, enhanced efficiency, and superior performance on conversational benchmarks, without relying on reference models or incurring length bias?
Hypothesis: A preference optimization algorithm that employs a reference-free, length-normalized reward aligned with the model's generation metric, and incorporates a target reward margin, will outperform existing reference-based and reference-free methods in both efficiency and alignment quality, while minimizing length exploitation.
Proposed Method: The proposed method, SimPO (Simple Preference Optimization), introduces a novel offline preference optimization objective for large language models. The approach replaces the traditional reward formulation with a reference-free, length-normalized reward: the average log probability of the generated sequence under the policy model, scaled by a constant β. This reward directly aligns with the metric used during model generation, eliminating the need for a reference model and thus reducing computational and memory overhead. Additionally, a target reward margin γ is incorporated into the Bradley-Terry objective, enforcing that the reward for the preferred (winning) response exceeds that of the non-preferred (losing) response by at least γ. The method is designed to prevent length bias by normalizing rewards by sequence length, and does not require explicit KL regularization to maintain generalization.
Novelty Claims: The proposed method eliminates the need for a reference model during preference optimization, significantly improving computational and memory efficiency. By aligning the reward function with the actual generation metric and introducing a target reward margin, the approach achieves superior alignment with human preferences and robust generalization, as evidenced by consistent and significant outperformance over existing baselines across multiple benchmarks. The method also effectively prevents length exploitation, a common issue in preference optimization, and demonstrates state-of-the-art results among open-source models under 10B parameters.


### Paper 5:
**WPO: Enhancing RLHF with Weighted Preference Optimization** (2024)
Research Question: How can preference optimization in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) be improved to better align large language models (LLMs) with human values, particularly in settings where preference data is collected off-policy?
Hypothesis: Reweighting preference pairs in off-policy RLHF according to their probability under the current policy will mitigate the distributional gap between data collection and target policy, leading to more effective and efficient preference optimization without incurring additional costs.
Proposed Method: A novel Weighted Preference Optimization (WPO) framework will be developed to simulate on-policy learning using off-policy preference data. The method assigns weights to each preference pair based on the joint probability of their outputs under the current policy, prioritizing pairs more likely to be generated by the policy model. To address variance and ensure fair weighting, length-normalized sequence probabilities and token-level alignment techniques (such as sampled and greedy alignment) will be employed. The approach can be integrated with various loss functions for preference optimization and supports both paired and unpaired preference data. The method will be implemented efficiently to avoid the computational cost of active on-policy sampling during training.
Novelty Claims: The proposed WPO method introduces a principled reweighting of off-policy preference data to closely simulate on-policy RLHF, effectively bridging the distributional gap without additional sampling costs. The approach is generalizable and can be incorporated into various preference optimization loss functions. Empirical results are expected to demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, achieving new best results on standard alignment benchmarks. The analysis will also provide new insights into the relative importance of on-policy versus off-policy data, and the roles of preferred and dispreferred samples in preference optimization.

## Proposed Research

**Preference Distillation via Value based Reinforcement Learning** (2025)
Research Question: How can small language models be more effectively aligned with human preferences using preference distillation, especially when limited to coarse-grained, binary feedback and lacking the capacity to fully leverage large teacher models?
Hypothesis: Incorporating a value-based auxiliary reward derived from a DPO-trained teacher model into the preference distillation process will provide more informative supervision, preserve the optimal policy, and lead to improved alignment and performance of small language models compared to existing distillation and preference optimization methods.
Proposed Method: A new preference distillation framework, Teacher Value-based Knowledge Distillation (TVKD), will be developed to enhance the alignment of small language models with human preferences. The method will extract the value function from a DPO-trained teacher model and use it to construct a potential-based reward shaping term, which is added as an auxiliary reward to the student's RL objective. This shaping term, defined as the difference in the teacher's value function between consecutive states, provides soft, sequence-level guidance without interfering with the global reward structure or optimal policy of DPO. The approach will be integrated into standard DPO training pipelines with minimal modification and will not require additional rollouts or online teacher queries, making it fully compatible with offline preference datasets.
Novelty Claims: The proposed method introduces the first use of a teacher's value function as a soft, sequence-level auxiliary reward for preference distillation in language models. By leveraging potential-based reward shaping, the approach ensures policy invariance and avoids conflicts with the original DPO objective, enabling the transfer of the teacher's internal reward modeling to the student. The framework is fully offline, requiring no additional rollouts, and demonstrates consistent improvements across model sizes, architectures, and diverse benchmarks. The method also provides theoretical and empirical evidence that value-based shaping outperforms action-dependent shaping and other auxiliary reward strategies in aligning small models with human preferences.
Experiment Details: Experiments will be conducted using several small language models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-1B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, Danube3-500M) as students and larger models (e.g., Mistral-7B-v0.2, LLaMA-3.1-8B) as teachers. Baselines for comparison will include various knowledge distillation methods (VanillaKD, DCKD, SeqKD, GKD), offline alignment methods (DPO, SimPO, WPO, TDPO), and other preference distillation approaches (DDPO, DPKD, ADPA). Metrics will include scalar reward model scores, win rates in pairwise comparisons, and average benchmark ratings. Ablation studies will be performed across different teacher-student model pairs and reward shaping strategies.

The methodology will involve (1) constructing a taxonomy of RLHF challenges, distinguishing between tractable issues and fundamental limitations; (2) developing and evaluating new techniques to improve the quality, representativeness, and robustness of human feedback, reward models, and policy learning; and (3) designing and proposing auditing and disclosure standards to enhance transparency and societal oversight of RLHF-trained systems. **Reward Model Ensembles Help Mitigate Overoptimization** (2023)
Research Question: Can ensemble-based conservative optimization methods mitigate the problem of overoptimization in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for fine-tuning large language models, particularly under realistic conditions such as label noise?

Proposed Method: The proposed approach involves training an ensemble of proxy reward models, each initialized with different random seeds but using the same data and hyperparameters. Policy optimization will be performed using both best-of-n sampling (BoN) and proximal policy optimization (PPO), with and without additional KL penalty terms. The method is designed to be robust to hyperparameters such as ensemble size and uncertainty penalty.

The approach demonstrates that WCO and UWO objectives can practically eliminate overoptimization and significantly improve performance, even in the presence of substantial label noise. The method is shown to be robust to hyperparameter choices and provides performance gains orthogonal to those achieved by increasing reward model size or dataset size. The findings suggest that ensemble-based conservative optimization is a scalable and cost-effective solution for improving RLHF robustness.

**AlpacaFarm: A Simulation Framework for Methods that Learn from Human Feedback** (2023)

The framework will use LLMs (such as GPT-4) as simulated annotators to generate pairwise preference data at a fraction of the cost of human annotation. Prompts and annotator pools will be designed to capture not only the quality judgments of humans but also their inter- and intra-annotator variability, including injected random noise to emulate real-world label noise. An automated evaluation protocol will be established, measuring model win-rates against a strong reference model (e.g., Davinci003) on a diverse set of instructions drawn from multiple open-source datasets, mimicking real-world user interactions. The framework will include validated reference implementations of several learning-from-feedback algorithms (such as PPO, best-of-n, expert iteration, DPO, Quark, and binary reward conditioning), enabling systematic comparison and rapid iteration.
Novelty Claims: The proposed framework introduces a low-cost, high-fidelity simulation environment for learning from human feedback, enabling rapid iteration and benchmarking of instruction-following models. It provides a validated protocol for simulating human pairwise feedback using LLMs, capturing both quality judgments and annotator variability. The approach offers an automated evaluation protocol closely correlated with real human feedback and releases reference implementations of multiple LPF algorithms. The framework demonstrates that method rankings and qualitative behaviors observed in simulation reliably transfer to real-world human feedback, substantially reducing the cost and time required for research in this domain.

**Is DPO Superior to PPO for LLM Alignment? A Comprehensive Study** (2024)

## Proposed Research

**Mitigating Reward Over-Optimization in RLHF via Behavior-Supported Regularization** (2025)
Research Question: How can reward over-optimization in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for large language models be effectively mitigated, particularly by addressing the extrapolation errors that arise when reward models evaluate out-of-distribution (OOD) responses?
Hypothesis: Regularizing the value function using a behavior-supported Bellman operator, which penalizes OOD actions based on the next-token distribution from the reward training dataset, will reduce OOD response generation during RLHF, thereby mitigating reward over-optimization and enabling convergence to the optimal in-distribution policy.
Proposed Method: A novel Behavior-Supported Policy Optimization (BSPO) algorithm is developed to address reward over-optimization in RLHF. The method defines the behavior policy as the next-token distribution derived from the reward model's training data, characterizing the in-distribution (ID) region. A behavior-supported Bellman operator is introduced to regularize the value function, penalizing all OOD values without affecting ID ones. The ScoreLM model is implemented to jointly predict both the reward and the behavior distribution, using a combined loss function that balances preference modeling and supervised next-token prediction. Policy optimization is performed by iteratively updating the policy within the ID region, guided by the regularized value estimates, and leveraging PPO with advantage estimates derived from the behavior-supported value function.
Novelty Claims: The proposed approach is the first to use value regularization, via a behavior-supported Bellman operator, to address reward over-optimization in RLHF by penalizing only OOD actions while preserving ID policy evaluation. The method introduces a principled way to detect and control OOD responses using the next-token distribution, enabling explicit modeling of the ID region and ensuring monotonic policy improvement until convergence to the optimal behavior-supported policy. The ScoreLM architecture provides a lightweight and effective implementation for joint reward and behavior distribution prediction. Empirical results demonstrate superior mitigation of reward over-optimization and improved policy performance compared to existing baselines, especially at larger KL divergences.
Experiment Details: Experiments are conducted in a synthetic RLHF setup, using a gold-standard reward model (Llama3-8B) and three proxy reward models of varying sizes (GPT-2-large 774M, TinyLlama 1.1B, ShearedLlama 2.7B), all trained on preference data from the UltraFeedback dataset. The initial policy is Alpaca-7B, and all algorithms are evaluated using the same proxy and gold models. Baselines include Standard PPO, PPO with KL penalty, Constrained PPO (CPPO), and two ensemble-based methods (ENS-UWO and ENS-WCO). Evaluation metrics include proxy reward, gold reward, win rate against the initial model, and the average number of behavior-unsupported (OOD) actions per response. The experimental setup tracks OOD generation, policy performance, and robustness to KL divergence constraints.
